title: Top 100+ Things to Do in Burlington
tagline: More than a hundred experiences, ranked. Argue with us.
intro:
Not a list of addresses — more than a hundred things to actually do, ranked by how essential each one is to Burlington specifically. An experience you can't have anywhere else beats one that's merely nice, which is why a creemee outranks some very good restaurants. Each entry links to the places involved; tap through for maps, hours, and the full details.

The top ten is the answer to "I have one day, what do I do." The rest is the answer to living here.

items.title: Stroll the bricks of Church Street
items.teaser: Four pedestrian blocks, buskers, a gear basement and a shop full of oddities
items.body: The Church Street Marketplace opened in 1981 as one of the first pedestrian malls of its kind in the country, and its four brick blocks hold over 100 shops, restaurants and local businesses, with street entertainers and cart vendors all year. Outdoor Gear Exchange at 37 Church Street keeps its consignment desk in the basement. Flora & Fauna at 70 Church Street sells taxidermy, fossils and oddities. Ben & Jerry's scoops at 36 Church Street, and Ben and Jerry opened their very first shop in 1978 in a renovated gas station on St. Paul Street, across from City Hall Park.

items.title: Watch the sun drop behind the Adirondacks
items.teaser: Boardwalk swings, an 1813 battery bluff, a quiet cemetery and a stone circle for the sun
items.body: Waterfront Park puts you at water level on the boardwalk, where the swinging benches are the coveted seats. Battery Park looks down from a high point over the lake and the distant Adirondacks, and it's named for the cannons that turned back a British naval attack in 1813. Lakeview Cemetery on North Avenue, a Victorian park cemetery opened in 1872, ends in a quiet strip of grass above the bike path and the lake. In the South End, the Earth Clock at Oakledge Park is a circle of 14 granite stones that tracks the sun along the horizon.

items.title: Bike the causeway out into the middle of the lake
items.teaser: A marble causeway into the lake, a bike ferry across the Cut and a vineyard beyond
items.body: Local Motion's Trailside Center at 1 Steele Street rents bikes and e-bikes right on the Island Line Trail, which leaves the pavement at Airport Park and heads out across the Colchester Causeway, a three mile lake crossing built of Rutland marble for the 1899 Island Line Railroad, with the Adirondacks and Green Mountains in view. The bike ferry crosses the 200 foot gap called the Cut on a suggested $5 donation each way and returns in May 2027. In South Hero, Snow Farm Vineyard hosts free Thursday concerts from June through early September.

items.title: Eat a maple creemee, then settle the argument
items.teaser: Waterfront windows, real maple sprinkles in Jericho and a Colchester drive-through
items.body: A creemee is Vermont's word for soft serve, and maple is the flavor to order. On the waterfront, Burlington Bay Market & Café at 125 Battery Street calls the Maple Creemee its best seller, and ECHO runs Champ's Legendary Creemees from May through early October. Palmer Lane Maple at 19 Old Pump Road in Jericho makes a Maple Sundae with pure Vermont syrup and its own real maple sprinkles, April to October. The Village Scoop, attached to the original Colchester schoolhouse, serves the Tornado as its local special.

items.title: Crawl the South End's taprooms
items.teaser: Conehead and a smoked Rauchbier on Pine Street, then cider and BBQ on Flynn Avenue
items.body: Four South End taprooms make an easy crawl. Zero Gravity's beer hall at 716 Pine Street pours the Citra-hopped Conehead IPA and the Green State Lager. Queen City Brewery at 703 Pine Street has served European and English styles since 2014 across a 50 year old mahogany bar, including a Rauchbier in the Bamberg tradition. On Flynn Avenue, Citizen Cider presses Vermont and New York apples behind its Press House Pub at 180, and Switchback at 160, 100% employee owned, runs a Beer Garden & Smokehouse with house-smoked BBQ.

items.title: Drink a beer by the lake at golden hour
items.teaser: Foam's patio looks west to the Adirondack Mountains, with its own bar in warm months
items.body: Foam Brewers has poured at 112 Lake Street since 2016, with a westward view over Lake Champlain to the Adirondack Mountains. The draft list rotates through sours, lagers and IPAs, like the Tranquil Pils, a German pilsner, with cheese and charcuterie on the side, and the patio gets its own bar in the warmer months. The brewhouse and cellar sit in plain view of the bar, and Foam says a weekday visit is the time to talk beer with the staff.

items.title: Shop the farmers markets, Saturday and Tuesday
items.teaser: Saturdays on Pine Street since 1980, Tuesdays in Dewey Park with Moroccan and Yemeni food
items.body: The Burlington Farmers Market has run on Saturdays since 1980, now 9 to 2 at 345 Pine Street from Mother's Day weekend through October, with farmers, specialty food producers and artisan crafts, plus a winter season, and the #5 bus stops every half hour. The Old North End Farmers Market, there since 1992, sets up on Tuesdays from 3 to 6:30 in Dewey Park, where Archibald, Spring and Walnut Streets meet, built around affordable food. Its 2026 vendors included Kalaat Moroccan Kitchen, Yalla Eats' Yemeni dishes and Tremolo's stone oven bread.

items.title: Lose a full day at Shelburne Museum
items.teaser: A 220 foot steamboat on the grounds, 39 buildings, and a ticket that's good for two days
items.body: Electra Havemeyer Webb founded Shelburne Museum in 1947 and moved historic buildings onto its grounds, a lighthouse, a jail, a covered bridge and the 220 foot steamboat Ticonderoga among them. Today the 45 acre campus holds 39 buildings and 22 gardens, with the Shaker design Round Barn, a 1920s carousel and Webb Gallery paintings by Andrew Wyeth and Winslow Homer. It's open daily 10 to 5 from May into late October, adults pay $27.50, Vermont residents $15, and tickets cover two consecutive days. Winter Lights runs evenings from late November.

items.title: Walk the Vanderbilt estate at Shelburne Farms
items.teaser: A day on 1,400 lakeside acres by donation, with cheddar made while you watch
items.body: Lila Webb, a Vanderbilt daughter, and her husband William Seward Webb bought 33 farms on Shelburne Point in the late 1800s and built a grand agricultural estate, now a 1,400 acre working farm, education nonprofit and National Historic Landmark. From mid-May to mid-October a day visit is by donation, with more than 10 miles of trails, the Children's Farmyard and cheesemakers turning Brown Swiss milk into cheddar at the Farm Barn. The Farm Store, once the estate's North Gatehouse, stays open year round, and the Inn serves dinner.

items.title: Meet the lake's residents at ECHO
items.teaser: Sturgeon, gar and mudpuppies from the lake, plus a 30 foot Champ to settle the question
items.body: ECHO, Leahy Center for Lake Champlain, at 1 College Street keeps over 50 native Lake Champlain species in live displays across three levels, from lake sturgeon and longnosed gar to mudpuppies and snapping turtles. Animal presentations at 11 and 2 daily bring out American eels, Eastern newts and more. The Champ exhibit covers the 1977 Mansi photo and P.T. Barnum's 1873 reward, beside a Champ sculpture over 30 feet long. It's open daily 10 to 5, year round, and adults pay $23, or $20 for Vermont residents.

items.title: Pick a city beach and get in the lake
items.teaser: The big one with showers, 1,500 feet of sand, a dog beach and a secluded rocky cove
items.body: Burlington has five official beaches on Lake Champlain, all free on foot or by bike. North Beach, off Institute Road, is the largest, with food concessions, showers, summer kayak and paddleboard rentals and a campground, and parking runs $3 an hour from May to mid-October. Leddy Beach stretches 1,500 feet with grills and free parking, and has no lifeguard. Texaco Beach, reached off the Greenway, is the city's only dedicated dog beach, open to dogs year round. Oakledge Cove is the most secluded, with rocky outcroppings and quiet sunsets.

items.title: Ride the Greenway end to end
items.teaser: Eight paved miles from Oakledge to the Winooski River, and in winter a lane left for skis
items.body: The Burlington Greenway is an eight mile paved path along Lake Champlain, from just before Oakledge Park in the South End to the pedestrian bridge over the Winooski River, where it continues north as the Island Line Trail, passing several major parks along the way. In winter the city plows the lake side and leaves the east side for skiing. Local Motion's Trailside Center at 1 Steele Street rents bikes, e-bikes, kids' trailers and adaptive bikes, with free helmets and locks on request, and full day rentals are due back by 6.

items.title: Walk out to the Champlain Thrust Fault at Rock Point
items.teaser: Older Cambrian rock stacked on younger shale, on free trails with a quick online pass
items.body: Rock Point is 130 acres of conserved land on the lake, a center of the Episcopal Church in Vermont since 1855, with over two miles of trails that are free and open to the public. It has one of North America's most visible exposures of a dolomite thrust fault. At Lone Rock Point, the Champlain Thrust Fault puts older Cambrian dolostone on top of younger Ordovician shale, dark gray with white calcite veins. Get the free pass first, park at Leddy Park, walk the bike path to the Holy Trinity Trail and mind the 60 foot cliffs.

items.title: See a show at the Flynn
items.teaser: A restored 1930 Art Deco house with 1,439 seats and over 200 shows a year
items.body: The Flynn opened on November 26, 1930, as Vermont's largest and most modern entertainment venue, built for vaudeville and movies, and its restoration starting in 1981 became one of the nation's most significant Art Deco restoration projects. Today the 1,439 seat Main Stage at 153 Main Street hosts Broadway, music, dance, comedy and family shows, Flynn Space seats about 200 for intimate and experimental work, and the Amy E. Tarrant Gallery sits off the lobby. The Flynn presents more than 200 performances a year and runs the Burlington Discover Jazz Festival every June.

items.title: Hear live music downtown, from jazz jam to dance floor
items.teaser: Weekly jazz and funk jams on College Street, then live bands and DJs on Church Street
items.body: The 126 at 126 College Street is a 21 and over cocktail room with music five nights a week, starting with Big Easy Tuesdays with Jon McBride, a Wednesday jazz jam led by the house band, saxophonist and UVM jazz professor Alex Stewart's quartet on Thursdays before a weekly funk jam, and jazz sets at 7 or 9 on Fridays and Saturdays. Red Square at 136 Church Street is the louder end of the night, a bar with live music and DJs that opens Thursday through Saturday.

items.title: Book one of downtown's big dinners
items.teaser: Mushroom toast, mock eel, a lamb cracker, or a $28 French bistro early bird
items.body: Hen of the Wood, beside Hotel Vermont at 55 Cherry Street, changes its menu daily, and its sample menu lists the Hen of the Woods Mushroom Toast. Honey Road at 156 Church Street serves Eastern Mediterranean mezze, like the Lamb Cracker, from chef Cara Tobin, a four time James Beard finalist. A Single Pebble at 133 Bank Street serves Chinese family style Wednesday through Saturday, and its Mock Eel is crispy shiitake glazed in ginger and soy. Leunig's Bistro, open since 1980 and now on the corner of Church and College, has a $28 two course early bird.

items.title: Climb Mt. Philo, then eat at Philo Ridge Farm
items.teaser: Vermont's first state park, a 968 foot summit you can hike or drive, and a farm lunch
items.body: Mt. Philo State Park in Charlotte became Vermont's first state park in 1924, and its 968 foot summit looks over the Lake Champlain Valley to New York's Adirondack Mountains. A three quarter mile trail climbs to the top, or you can drive the summit road, and day use is $5 for adults from Memorial Day weekend into October. The park is noted for raptor watching and autumn bird migrations. Philo Ridge Farm at 2766 Mount Philo Road, a nonprofit on 500 acres, runs a Market and serves walk-in lunch Wednesday through Saturday.

items.title: Earn the summit of Camel's Hump
items.teaser: Free to hike, rare alpine plants up top, and get to the Burrows lot by 8 on weekends
items.body: Camel's Hump tops out at 4,083 feet and is one of just three Vermont summits with fragile arctic alpine plants. The state park is free and undeveloped. The popular Burrows Trail starts at the end of Camel's Hump Road in Huntington and meets the Long Trail for the summit, with 360 degree views, and the Monroe Trail climbs from Duxbury. Trails open the weekend before Memorial Day, and the Green Mountain Club says carry a paper map. A B-24 bomber hit its south face in October 1944. On a good weather weekend, get to the lot early, around 8, since cars parked along the road get towed.

items.title: Get to the top of Mount Mansfield, any way you like
items.teaser: Hike Sunset Ridge from Underhill, ride the Stowe gondola or drive the Toll Road
items.body: Mount Mansfield holds Vermont's highest point, the Chin at 4,395 feet, and the state's largest alpine zone, about 100 acres of rare plants. Of its 28 trails, the Long Trail runs the ridge, and the Stowe gondola with the Cliff House Trail or the Stowe Toll Road gets you up without the full climb, per the Green Mountain Club. Underhill State Park sits at about 2,000 feet on the west slope, home to the 3 mile Sunset Ridge Trail and a CCC-built pavilion, with $5 day use from Memorial Day weekend to the second Monday in October.

items.title: Get out on the lake by sailboat or cruise boat
items.teaser: A BYO picnic sail on a classic sloop from $68, or the big boat's narrated scenic cruise
items.body: Two outfits leave from 1 College Street on the waterfront. Whistling Man Schooner Co. sails classic sloops like Friend Ship and Wild Rose from slips 35 and 36 at the Burlington Community Boathouse on two hour cruises, daily from mid-May to mid-October, with shared seats from $68 on cruises that typically carry six to ten guests plus a captain and deckhand, and you bring your own food and drinks. The Spirit of Ethan Allen runs bigger cruises, from a narrated scenic cruise at $36.99 for adults in 2026 to nightly sunset cruises, with DJs on summer Fridays and Saturdays.

items.title: Eat dinner practically in the lake
items.teaser: Tacos on the Boathouse docks, lobster rolls on King Street, seafood in an 1833 building
items.body: Burlington's waterfront dining runs from dockside to old timber. Splash at the Boathouse serves tacos, wraps, burgers and a full bar on the docks of the Burlington Boathouse, from 11 until sunset in season, and it's dog friendly. Spot on the Dock at 1 King Street brings surf shack energy and lobster rolls from mid May to late September. Shanty on the Shore at 181 Battery Street cooks seafood in a building Isaac Nye put up as a store in 1833, the Shanty since 1985. The Skinny Pancake at 60 Lake Street does crepes from 7:30 every morning.

items.title: Make a night of comedy and games
items.teaser: 700 board games for $6, a 140 seat comedy room, then Galaga and pinball until late
items.body: Three stops cover the whole night. The Boardroom at 3 Mill Street has more than 700 board games to play for $6 a person, with grilled cheese, a bucket of Bugles and craft beer. Vermont Comedy Club at 101 Main Street seats 140 at cabaret tables, brings touring headliners Thursday through Saturday, and on Wednesdays runs a $5 improv night at 6:30 and a free standup open mic at 8:30. The Archives at 191 College Street is an arcade bar with 24 rotating taps and vintage cabinets like Tapper, Galaga, Pac-Man, NBA Jam and Attack from Mars pinball.

items.title: Catch a touring act at Higher Ground
items.teaser: Over 300 shows a year on Williston Road, from the crew that's backed Noah Kahan and Phish
items.body: Higher Ground has been bringing bands to the Burlington area since 1998, first in Winooski and now at 1214 Williston Road in South Burlington. It produces over 300 shows a year in Northern Vermont, and the artists it has supported include Noah Kahan, Anais Mitchell, Grace Potter and Phish. The same crew also books shows at Shelburne Museum, the Midway Lawn at CVE and Waterfront Park.

items.title: Watch the sap boil at a Vermont sugarhouse
items.teaser: Sugar on snow comes with a donut and a pickle, and Bragg's sugarhouse tours are free
items.body: Vermont maple is best seen at the source in March and April. Palmer's Sugarhouse in Shelburne, family run for over 50 years, offers maple demonstrations, free samples and traditional sugar on snow in season. Morse Farm Maple Sugarworks at 1168 County Road in Montpelier, an agritourism stop since 1966, opens its sugarhouse to the public in sugaring season and serves sugar on snow with a donut and a pickle. Bragg Farm in East Montpelier boils with buckets and a wood fired evaporator and gives free sugarhouse tours. Maple Open House Weekend is March 20 and 21, 2027.

items.title: Eat breakfast at a classic diner
items.teaser: A 1925 dining car on Bank Street, a horseshoe counter on Maple, a 1950s car out of town
items.body: Burlington still has real diners. Henry's Diner opened on Bank Street in June 1925 in a railroad dining car brought from Bayonne, New Jersey, and its homemade corned beef hash comes with 2 eggs any style. Handy's Lunch at 74 Maple Street, open since 1945, is run by the third generation of Handys around a horseshoe counter, home of the Chuck Norris, five slices of French toast with four eggs, bacon, ham, sausage, a burger and corned beef. The Parkway Diner on Williston Road has served in its original 1950s dining car since 1950, with biscuits made in house.

items.title: Walk the rocky shoreline at Red Rocks Park
items.teaser: 100 acres of hemlock and pine that open onto a rocky shore over Shelburne Bay
items.body: Red Rocks Park is 100 acres of South Burlington woods at 4 Central Avenue, open dawn to dusk all year. About 3.3 miles of trails loop through hemlock and pine and come out on a rocky shoreline with views of Lake Champlain, Shelburne Bay and the Adirondacks. The beach is open to the public with no lifeguards, and the city tests the water for E. coli every Monday and Wednesday in season. Bikes stay off the foot trails. In winter the same 100 acres take snowshoes and cross country skis.

items.title: Climb the treehouse at Oakledge Park
items.teaser: A 2004 treehouse up in a red oak, built so a wheelchair can roll right in
items.body: Oakledge is the biggest park in Burlington's South End, at the west end of Flynn Avenue with the Burlington Greenway running right through it. Its treehouse, built in 2004 by the Tree House Guys of Waitsfield and billed as the world's first universally accessible treehouse, is a 500 square foot platform up in a red oak, reached by a wooden pier off the ledge. Around it are two beaches, rocky lakeside cliffs, a playground with universal access features, bocce and tennis courts, and the Upper and Lower Wetland, good for watching birds.

items.title: Walk under the girders of the Moran Frame
items.teaser: A 1954 coal plant stripped down to its steel and painted a striking red
items.body: The Moran Frame is the steel skeleton of the Moran Municipal Generating Station, a 30 megawatt coal plant that opened on Burlington's northern waterfront in 1954, switched to wood chips in 1977 and was decommissioned in 1986. In 2022 and 2023 the city peeled off the brick to reveal the steel superstructure, kept its tiered shape and painted it a striking red, beside Lake Champlain. It is now an open air public park. Friends of the FRAME puts on free events there, and two custom swinging benches hang in the northwest bay.

items.title: Wander the halls of the old Soda Plant
items.teaser: Coffee at a roastery, a gallery out back, and a $5 ginger ale where it was first bottled
items.body: The Soda Plant at 266 Pine Street is where Venetian ginger ale was first bottled in 1917, and today it holds South End studios, a gallery and small businesses. Brio Coffeeworks, a woman owned specialty roaster, runs its roastery and coffee bar inside. The S.P.A.C.E. Gallery shows local art Thursday through Saturday from 12 to 5, with First Friday receptions. Venetian Soda Lounge, a 48 seat speakeasy that opened in 2022, pours cocktails and $5 house sodas, including ginger ale, with live jazz, blues and folk most nights it's open.

items.title: Hop between galleries on Church Street
items.teaser: Three floors of rotating shows, then the first state craft center in the nation
items.body: Two stops on Church Street cover Vermont art from both ends. The BCA Center at 135 Church Street is Burlington City Arts' three level, year round exhibition space, open Wednesday through Saturday from noon and until 8 on Wednesdays and Saturdays. Frog Hollow at 85 Church Street, founded in 1971 and named the first state craft center in the nation in 1975, sells the work of over 100 Vermont artists, from fine traditional craft to contemporary art.

items.title: Cheer on a home team on a summer night
items.teaser: Back to back national champions at Virtue Field, and baseball in a ballpark from 1906
items.body: Burlington's summer sports happen on two fields near UVM. Vermont Green FC plays at Virtue Field on the UVM campus from early May to mid July, and won the USL League Two national title in 2025 and again in 2026. When the bleachers sell out, the hill is free, and the supporters, the Green Mountain Bhoys among them, make their voices heard. The Vermont Lake Monsters play summer collegiate baseball in the Futures League at Centennial Field, 287 Colchester Avenue, which opened in 1906 and got its main grandstand in 1922. Parking is $5 and Champ is the mascot.

items.title: Pack the stands at a winter UVM game
items.teaser: Hockey East in a 4,007 seat rink from 1963, and America East's preseason favorite
items.body: UVM's two big winter tickets share 97 Spear Street. Gutterson Fieldhouse opened in 1963, holds 4,007 for Catamount hockey in Hockey East, sent the program to its first Frozen Four in 1996, and has long been one of the toughest places in college hockey for visiting teams. Patrick Gymnasium has been home to Catamount basketball since 1963, and the men were picked as the 2026-27 America East preseason favorite, the 10th time in 11 seasons. Everyone 3 and older needs a ticket.

items.title: Plan a weekend around a Burlington festival
items.teaser: Jazz in June, beer on the waterfront in July, and Art Hop the weekend after Labor Day
items.body: Three festivals are worth planning a weekend around. The Burlington Discover Jazz Festival, run by the Flynn, fills five days each June with mostly free shows, including free headline sets on the waterfront, and its 44th edition is set for June 2 to 6, 2027. The Vermont Brewers Festival takes over Waterfront Park in July with over 40 breweries, at $60 in advance for a 2026 session, 21 and over. The South End Art Hop fills more than 125 locations along 1.5 miles of Pine Street the weekend after Labor Day, free to attend.

items.title: Pick your own fruit from June to October
items.teaser: Organic strawberries in June, cherries in July, then apples and Dead Bird brandy by fall
items.body: Picking season runs from strawberries in June to apples in October. Adam's Berry Farm in Charlotte grows certified organic strawberries, raspberries and blueberries on 57 acres of conserved land, with blueberries from late July. Champlain Orchards in Shoreham, one of the oldest continually operating orchards in Vermont, grows over 175 varieties and runs pick your own from cherries in late June through peaches in August to apples in October. Shelburne Orchards opens its 60 acres for apple picking in September and October, with cider doughnuts, fresh pressed cider and its own Dead Bird apple brandy.

items.title: Drop down to Salmon Hole on the Winooski River
items.teaser: Where spawning salmon gather below the dam, on rock rippled about 500 million years ago
items.body: Salmon Hole is a 6 acre Winooski Valley Park District park off Riverside Avenue in Burlington, just before the bridge to Winooski. It takes its name from the spawning salmon that gather in the swirling pool below the Winooski One Hydro dam. The rocks here are rippled by water currents that covered the land about 500 million years ago, with striations in the cliff side, and the Riverwalk Trail follows the Winooski River from here to a viewing area off Intervale Road.

items.title: Eat from the food trucks on a warm evening
items.teaser: Fridays on Pine Street with 70 plus vendors, then a beer garden that moves parks
items.body: The South End Get Down is a free block party on Pine Street every Friday night of the summer from 5 to 9, with more than 70 food vendors over the season curated by Food Trucks of Vermont, DJs, and The Pinery beer garden. The vendor list goes up on Instagram on Friday mornings, Local Motion runs free valet bike parking, and leashed dogs are welcome. In September, South Burlington's Park Hop Brews sets up a traveling beer garden in a different city park every Thursday from 5:30 to 7:30, with music, food vendors and games.

items.title: Cross the river for a Winooski night out
items.teaser: Dinner in a 1912 mill over the river, a brewery biergarden, then a band on Main Street
items.body: Winooski packs a full night around Main Street. Waterworks Food + Drink sits in the Champlain Mill, completed in 1912 as Mill No. 4 for the American Woolen Company, serving creative American food from 4:30 with a view of the Winooski River from nearly every seat. Four Quarters Brewing, founded in 2014, now runs a restaurant and heated biergarden at 70 Main Street, pouring beers like the Space Face double IPA. The Monkey House at 30 Main Street is a small music venue, neighborhood bar and pizza shop, with Monday trivia and band tickets that often run $10 to $15.

items.title: Eat around the world in the Old North End
items.teaser: Pho in an old bus station, al pastor on fresh corn tortillas, shawarma until midnight
items.body: The Old North End eats its way around the world. Pho Hong opened in 2008 in a converted bus station at 325 North Winooski Avenue, a family Vietnamese kitchen where regulars order by number. Taco Gordo began as a taco cart in 2014 and opened its restaurant in the neighborhood in December 2018, with tacos served on two fresh corn tortillas, spit roasted al pastor and a cashew milk horchata. The Wise Fool at 260 North Street seats 25 and serves shawarma in laffa, a big Iraqi flatbread, until 11, or midnight on Friday and Saturday.

items.title: Go on a sandwich hunt around Burlington
items.teaser: Cash only lamb in a stone cellar, a pork belly banh mi, and Martone's big sandwiches
items.body: Three delis make the case. Four Corners of the Earth has spent over 25 years in the red stone cellar of the Kilburn & Gates building at 310 Pine Street, building globally named sandwiches like the Lebanese Lamb, toasted at the end with its house Sahara seasoning, and it's cash only. Henry Street Deli at 11 Henry Street does a banh mi with roasted coriander pork belly, pickled carrot and daikon. Martone's Market at 16 Main Street in Essex Junction has cut Boar's Head meats to order since 1992, known for big sandwiches and its Monster Deli Pickle.

items.title: Settle Burlington's bagel argument
items.teaser: Wood fired Montreal style on Shelburne Road or New York style on Pine Street
items.body: Burlington has a real bagel debate. Myer's Bagels at 408 Shelburne Road has hand rolled Montreal style bagels and baked them in a wood fired oven since 1997, inspired by St-Viateur Bagel in Montreal, and it opens at 6. Feldman's Bagels at 660 Pine Street keeps up the New York style bagels and bialys Roy Feldman brought to Vermont in 1979, with no white sugar or dough conditioners. Willow's Bagels, behind City Market at 71 South Union Street, boils and bakes handmade bagels every day from 7:30. All three close at 2.

items.title: Get a cup of Al's French Frys and a creemee
items.teaser: A cup of frys is $3.26 at the Williston Road stand that dates to 1946
items.body: Al's French Frys calls itself a Burlington tradition since 1946, started by Al and Genevieve Rusterholz, and the James Beard Foundation named it an America's Classic in 2010. The South Burlington stand at 1251 Williston Road began as an open counter with no seats, and the owners say the frys are still the same. A cup is $3.26, a pint $4.96 and a quart $8.94, with cheese, gravy or chili on top, plus burgers and Vermont creemees. It's open until 11, and until midnight on Friday and Saturday.

items.title: Settle in for a long brunch
items.teaser: Red flannel hash at Hotel Vermont, Penny Cluse classics by the lake, Kahlua French toast
items.body: Juniper, Hotel Vermont's lobby restaurant at 41 Cherry Street, serves brunch every day from 7 until 11, and until 1 on Saturday and Sunday, and Resy takes reservations. The red flannel hash with Jericho Settlers Farm beets and Montreal-spiced brisket is $20. Deep City at 112 Lake Street, next to Foam, serves brunch Thursday through Monday from a menu by Charles Reeves, founder of Penny Cluse, walk-ins only. Across the river at 28 Main Street in Winooski, Sneakers Bistro has served breakfast since 1980, with Kahlua French toast and its Famous Eggs Benedict, and you can join its line online.

items.title: Pick a side in Burlington's pizza debate
items.teaser: Neapolitan at Verità, house beer with flatbread, or BYOB sourdough next to Fiddlehead
items.body: Two of the city's pizza camps share Saint Paul Street. Pizzeria Verità, at 156 since 2012, bakes Neapolitan pies in a very hot wood-fired oven with fior di latte made in house, and its $17 Margherita is $5 off every Wednesday. American Flatbread's Burlington Hearth, at 115 since 2004, brews all of its beer in house, and Zero Gravity began there as its brewpub. Out in Shelburne, the original Folino's at 6305 Shelburne Road bakes naturally leavened sourdough pies at 650 to 700 degrees, is BYOB, and shares a building with the Fiddlehead tasting room.

items.title: Drink downtown like a regular
items.teaser: Vermont's first brewpub, then the pool bar its old head brewer opened in 1995
items.body: The Vermont Pub & Brewery at 144 College Street, founded by Greg Noonan, opened in late 1988 as the state's first brewpub and still pours Burly Irish Ale, with 15% off food on Tuesday for a Vermont or Canadian ID. Glenn Walter spent 6 years as its head brewer before opening Three Needs in 1995 as Burlington's first exclusive craft beer bar. Three Needs, at 185 Pearl Street, is open daily 4 to 2, with pool tables, a courtyard of couches and New Jersey boardwalk-style slices from the Pizza Cube, Tuesday through Saturday.

items.title: Play unlimited pinball at the Pinball Co-op
items.teaser: $15 buys a whole night on up to 36 machines, Wednesday and Friday from 6 to 10
items.body: The Pinball Co-op fills a back room at 1881 Williston Road in South Burlington, behind the white building with the 802 Fusion sign, with up to 36 fully working machines that change often. Open play runs Wednesday and Friday from 6 to 10, and $15 covers all you can play. Wednesday is league night, when league players get first pick of games, and the co-op calls Friday its fun day. It's BYOB, with a fridge, a lounge and a few arcade games, and its leagues and monthly tournaments need no experience.

items.title: Climb the walls at Petra Cliffs
items.teaser: A $23 day pass, a $10 gear package and a $10 belay lesson, no reservation needed
items.body: Petra Cliffs has been Burlington's climbing gym since 2000 and sits at 105 Briggs Street, with 15+ auto belay routes, 50+ top rope and lead routes and 100+ boulder routes. An adult day pass is $23 and good all day, so you can leave and come back, and shoes, harness and chalk rent as a $10 package, before tax. First timers get a safety orientation, and a belay lesson is $10 with no reservation. It's open 10 to 10 on weekdays, 10 to 8 Saturday and 10 to 6 Sunday.

items.title: Skate the waterfront park Tony Hawk endorsed
items.teaser: A 21,000 square foot concrete park with a bowl that drops to 10 feet, right on the lake
items.body: The Andy A-Dog Williams Skatepark is a 21,000 square foot concrete park on the Lake Champlain waterfront, designed by Grindline and built by Artisan Skateparks, with a flowing street section around a bowl that drops to 10 feet. It's named for A-Dog, a local skater, DJ and artist who helped build the city's earlier temporary park and died in 2013. The park came out of more than ten years of grassroots advocacy, a $10,000 Tony Hawk Foundation grant in 2010 pushed it forward, and Hawk spun a 540 in the bowl at the 2016 naming ceremony, the 500th park his foundation helped open.

items.title: Watch a drive-in movie or a free waterfront classic
items.teaser: A drive-in running since 1948, free classics every other Tuesday, and VTIFF each October
items.body: The Sunset Drive-In in Colchester has shown movies since 1948 and runs 4 screens. Downtown, Main Street Landing runs a free classic film series every other Tuesday at 7 at its Film House, on the third floor of the Lake and College Building at 60 Lake Street, on a 25 foot screen with Dolby surround, with donations at the door going to a local nonprofit. The same address is home to the Vermont International Film Festival, VTIFF, founded in 1985, which holds its festival each October, screens films at the Film House through the year and lets members in free.

items.title: Warm up downtown on a freezing night
items.teaser: Hot chocolate on Pine, tonkotsu on Church Street, then a downstairs bar with a fireplace
items.body: Lake Champlain Chocolates' flagship at 750 Pine Street is open daily 9 to 6, with free samples, a view of the Innovation Kitchen, a café pouring what it bills as America's Best hot chocolate, and a $16 guided tasting. Gaku Ramen opened on Church Street in June 2016 and serves a pork tonkotsu broth cooked for hours, plus miso and shoyu, at 144 Church Street, open late Thursday through Saturday. Farmhouse Tap & Grill at 160 Bank Street, open 11 to 10 daily, has a downstairs bar, the Parlor, pouring Vermont craft beer by a fireplace.

items.title: Join the 3 AM slice line on Main Street
items.teaser: Mr. Mike's serves slices until 3 on weekend nights, and Kountry Kart opens at 6:30
items.body: Mr. Mike's Pizza at 206 Main Street keeps its counter open until 3 in the morning on Friday and Saturday nights, and until 10 the rest of the week, which makes it a natural closing time stop. Kountry Kart Deli, next to the Flynn at 155 Main Street since 1989, handles the morning after, opening at 6:30 every day with its Shiner breakfast sandwiches, the Mikster sub named for founder Mike and the Hobo burger, a hand-formed patty with a fried egg on top.

items.title: Do the coffee crawl
items.teaser: A laptop free bakery, a single origin bar, Pine Street's roaster and coffee with ice cream
items.body: August First at 149 S. Champlain Street has been laptop free since 2014 and serves breakfast all day, 7:30 to 3. Onyx Tonics at 126 College Street, open since 2016, pours a weekly menu of 6 or more single origin coffees, and Jason Gonzalez, who runs it, is a two-time UK Cup Tasting Champion. Speeder & Earl's, a family roastery since 1993, runs its café at 412 Pine Street in the South End. Scout pairs curated coffee with homemade ice cream on Pine Street, on North Avenue and in Winooski.

items.title: Hike a smaller mountain with a big view
items.teaser: A fire tower at Elmore, an old hotel road up Snake Mountain, or Stowe Pinnacle's bald top
items.body: Elmore Mountain rises above Lake Elmore in Elmore State Park to 2,608 feet, with a fire tower on top. The 1.7 mile Fire Tower Trail and the 2.3 mile Ridge Trail, past Balancing Rock, make a loop of about 4 miles. Snake Mountain in Addison tops out at 1,287 feet via the 1.8 mile Arthur Gibb Trail, an old carriage road to an 1870 hotel, looking across the Champlain Valley to the Adirondacks. The Stowe Pinnacle Trail in Stowe climbs short and steep to a bald summit facing Mount Mansfield, just under 5 miles round trip.

items.title: Climb Ethan Allen Tower
items.teaser: A 1905 tower in a New North End woods with views from the lake to Mt. Mansfield
items.body: Ethan Allen Park, off North Avenue at Ethan Allen Parkway, is one of the first urban forest parks in the United States, on land Ethan Allen once owned. Its observation tower went up in 1905 thanks to Mayor William Van Patten and looks out from Lake Champlain to Mt. Mansfield. City volunteer Keypers open and close it, weekends from Mother's Day to Indigenous Peoples' Day and weekdays Memorial Day to Labor Day. Dirt trails loop the cliffs, and Ethan Allen Pinnacle at the north end has a gazebo and a view to Grand Isle.

items.title: Tour Ethan Allen's homestead
items.teaser: His 1785 house, a recreated Abenaki village and 4 miles of river trails, May to October
items.body: The Ethan Allen Homestead Museum centers on the 1785 house that was Ethan Allen's last home. The Allen House opens only for guided tours of about an hour, daily at 10:30, 11:50, 1:10 and 2:30 from May 1 to October 31, a 150 yard walk from the barn visitor center, so arrive 30 minutes early for a short film. Adults pay $15. Fanny's Garden, Negôni Alnôbaakik, a recreated Abenaki village, and over 4 miles of trails linking to the Intervale surround it, and the trails stay open when the museum closes, November through April.

items.title: Walk the Intervale's farm trails
items.teaser: 360 acres of farmland and river trails, open every day of the year and skiable in winter
items.body: The Intervale Center, founded in 1988 and an early force behind community supported agriculture, manages a 360 acre campus of farmland, trails and open space along the Winooski River at 180 Intervale Road, open to the public 365 days a year. Its trails, including the Rena Calkins Trail along the river, run all the way to the Ethan Allen Homestead and suit walking, biking, birding and jogging, with 3+ miles of ungroomed cross country ski trails in winter. Tommy Thompson Community Gardens, Burlington's largest with 150 plots, is here too.

items.title: Spend an hour at the Fleming
items.teaser: UVM's free art museum, 25,000 works across 5,000 years, open September to May
items.body: The Fleming Museum of Art at 61 Colchester Avenue, on UVM's campus next to the Medical Center, opened in 1931 and holds about 25,000 works of art and cultural heritage items from around the world, spanning more than 5,000 years, with only about 4% on view at a time. It's free, with a suggested $5 donation. It follows the academic year, open September to May, Tuesday through Friday from 10 (until 7 on Wednesday, 4 otherwise) and Saturday 12 to 4, and closes over UVM breaks. Sketching in pencil is welcome.

items.title: Spend a rainy hour in the Carnegie library
items.teaser: Andrew Carnegie paid for it in 1901, and it opens its doors every day of the week
items.body: The Fletcher Free Library at 235 College Street, one block east of Church Street, began with a $20,000 gift from Mary L. Fletcher and her daughter Mary M. Fletcher in 1873. Andrew Carnegie gave $50,000 in 1901 for the building that opened on August 17, 1904, now on the National Register of Historic Places, and an exterior restoration of its 1904 windows, brick and terracotta wrapped up in summer 2026. It offers free internet and over 155,000 items, and it's open every day, from noon on Sunday and until 8 on Tuesday and Wednesday.

items.title: Do the bookstore crawl
items.teaser: Phoenix and Crow on Church Street, then tens of thousands of used books on Pine
items.body: Phoenix Books at 89 Church Street sells new books, keeps a Vermont Authors & Illustrators section and hosts in-store events like a poetry open mic, open until 8 Monday through Saturday. Crow Bookshop at 14 Church Street has served the Marketplace for 30 years, mixing new, used and bargain books with an Old & Interesting section of antiquarian finds. Speaking Volumes at 377 Pine Street in the South End holds tens of thousands of used titles, rare, vintage, antiquarian and modern, with ephemera, art, antiques and magazines between the shelves.

items.title: Go on a vintage safari
items.teaser: Mid century finds on Pine, a reuse shop that haggles, and 60 dealers under one roof
items.body: Barge Canal Market at 377 Pine Street in the South End sells antique and vintage furnishings, focused on mid 20th century design, American industrial and vintage farmhouse. Check its Facebook page before you go. Junktiques Collective at 324 N. Winooski Avenue in the Old North End is a reuse shop of low cost goods and artists' materials that encourages barter, trades and haggling, open Wednesday to Saturday 11 to 7 and Sunday 12 to 5. Vintage Inspired Marketplace at 10 Dorset Street in South Burlington gathers over 60 vendors and is open until 6 every day.

items.title: Flip through the record stores
items.teaser: New and used vinyl on College Street, then a Winooski shop that runs its own label
items.body: Burlington Records at 194 College Street buys and sells new and used vinyl, keeps its used stock in the shop, flattens warped records, and is open daily from 10, until 7 most days and later Thursday through Saturday. Autumn Records at 11 E. Allen Street, Suite 2, at the top of the Winooski circle, buys, sells and trades vinyl, CDs, cassettes and stereo gear, looks for used collections from the 1950s on, and is open noon to 6 every day. It also has its own record label and a $40 a month subscription of one new and one used record.

items.title: Pack a local picnic and eat it by the lake
items.teaser: Over 100 local vendors at the co-op, plus Miss Weinerz sourdough donuts
items.body: City Market, Onion River Co-op has been Burlington's community owned grocery since 1973, and everyone is welcome to shop, member or not. The downtown store at 82 South Winooski Ave is open 7 am to 9 pm daily, with Vermont made food from over 100 local vendors, bread from more than 30 local bakeries, a sandwich station and a hot bar from 11 to 7. Wednesday through Sunday it also carries Miss Weinerz, the New North End home bakery whose vegan sourdough donuts use fresh milled Vermont wheat. Carry the bag down to Waterfront Park.

items.title: Watch glass get blown at AO Glass
items.teaser: Free to watch Monday to Saturday, or $175 to blow your own bowl or vase
items.body: AO Glass is a family owned glass studio at 416 Pine Street, directly behind Speeder & Earl's, where glassblowing is free to watch and the store sits right inside the studio. It's open Monday through Saturday from 10 to 3, until 4 Wednesday through Friday. The designs draw on the founders' Scandinavian and Italian influences, including Graal glass, a technique Orrefors of Sweden developed in 1916. For $175 a person, a one hour class pairs you with one of their gaffers to make a bowl, vase or tumbler, ages 16 and up, ready to pick up the next day.

items.title: Tour the Teddy Bear factory and Bear Hospital
items.teaser: A $6 tour that ends at the Bear Hospital, where Dr. Pam fixes bears guaranteed for life
items.body: The Vermont Teddy Bear factory at 6655 Shelburne Road is open 10 to 4 daily and runs guided tours for $6 for adults, $5 for seniors and $2 for kids 3 to 12. The tour starts in the Bear-racks, walks the assembly line where heads and limbs are stuffed with recycled plastic water bottles, and ends at the Bear Hospital, where Dr. Pam treats bears that are guaranteed for life, peanut allergies and all. Kids can build their own in the Design Studio, there are picnic tables outside, and dogs and cats are invited on the tour.

items.title: Taste cold climate wine and Vermont cider
items.teaser: Five wine flights for $18 in Shelburne, then bone dry cider in a Stowe cider garden
items.body: Shelburne Vineyard planted its first grapes in 1998 and grows mostly cold hardy hybrids like Marquette, La Crescent and Louise Swenson, plus a little Riesling. The tasting room at 6308 Shelburne Road opens daily at noon and pours two five wine flights for $18 each, waived with a two bottle purchase, one of them a sweet wine and ice cider flight. Stowe Cider at 17 Town Farm Lane in Stowe is open Wednesday through Sunday from noon to 9, with High & Dry, taproom only releases, a cider garden, barbecue and live music.

items.title: Make a Vermont beer pilgrimage
items.teaser: Heady Topper at the source, von Trapp lagers, and a farm brewery in Greensboro Bend
items.body: The Alchemist opened its Stowe brewery at 100 Cottage Club Road in 2016, and the Beer Cafe pours Heady Topper, an American double IPA, on draft from 11 every day, with $25 tours for ages 21 and up. Von Trapp Brewing at 1333 Luce Hill Road serves Austrian style lagers, starting with its original Helles, in a Bierhall open daily 11:30 to 9. Hill Farmstead, founded in 2010 on the Hill family's land at 403 Hill Road in Greensboro Bend in the Northeast Kingdom, opens its taproom and retail shop at 11:30 Wednesday through Sunday.

items.title: Eat through Waterbury, from cider donuts to barbecue
items.teaser: Fresh cider donuts, the Flavor Graveyard, then smoked meats on Main Street
items.body: Cold Hollow Cider Mill at 3600 Waterbury-Stowe Road in Waterbury Center has been a working cider mill since 1974, open 8 to 6 daily, where you can watch cider pressed and eat donuts made fresh daily. The Ben & Jerry's factory, built in 1985, runs a 30 minute tour with a MOO-vie, a view of the production floor and a tasting in the Flavor Room, $6 for adults, with tickets released 14 days ahead. It has sold out daily since reopening. The Flavor Graveyard is seasonal. Prohibition Pig smokes meats on Main Street, with its brewery around the corner open seven days a week for lunch and dinner.

items.title: Taste Vermont cheese where it's made
items.teaser: Goat cheese washed with local beer, a farm store in a barn, and Cabot's own shop
items.body: Sage Farm Goat Dairy in Stowe is run by sisters Molly and Katie Pindell, who milk Alpine goats and make cheese March through December. Its self serve farm store at 2346 West Hill Road opens daily at 9, April through November, with cheeses like Spruce, wrapped in spruce bark, and Lightning Knoll, washed with beers including Heady Topper. Von Trapp Farmstead at 251 Common Road in Waitsfield makes organic cheese and sells it from a farm store built into its barn, open year round. The Cabot Creamery Store in Waterbury Center opens Tuesday through Sunday at 10:30.

items.title: Sip spirits distilled in Vermont
items.teaser: Flights on St. Paul Street, a Church Street tasting room, and free tours at Barr Hill
items.body: Mad River Distillers makes whiskey, rum and apple brandy in Warren and pours flights and cocktails at its tasting room at 137 St. Paul Street, open daily from noon, until 8 Thursday through Saturday. Smugglers' Notch Distillery, founded in 2006, bottles its spirits one small batch at a time and pours them at 28 Church Street, open daily 11 to 7. Barr Hill at 116 Gin Lane in Montpelier is the only place its gin and vodka are distilled, with a James Beard nominated bar, weekend lunch until 3:30 and free 15 minute tours Sunday through Friday.

items.title: Cool off in a Vermont swimming hole
items.teaser: Deep pools at Warren Falls, a cave behind Bartlett Falls, a protected brook in Johnson
items.body: Warren Falls, on Green Mountain National Forest land less than 2 miles south of Warren village on Route 100, has high cliffs, fast water and deep swimming holes on the Mad River, plus a parking area on the west side of the highway. Never park on Route 100 itself. Bartlett Falls in Bristol is a 15 foot waterfall on the New Haven River off Lincoln Road with a cave behind it, and State Police have towed cars blocking that road. Journey's End in Johnson protects a half mile of Foote Brook on town land, with a pull-off on Plot Road.

items.title: Take a short walk to a waterfall
items.teaser: A 125 foot cascade in Stowe, a gorge off Route 108, and glacial potholes in Hancock
items.body: Moss Glen Falls in Stowe cascades 125 feet through a gorge, about a quarter mile in on a trail with bog bridging over the wet parts, from a parking area on Moss Glen Falls Road. Bingham Falls, part of Smugglers' Notch State Park, is a quarter mile walk down from two paved pull-offs on Route 108, steep and slippery at the bottom, with roped gorge edges where a fall can be fatal. Texas Falls in Hancock spills over potholes carved by glacial meltwater, on a 1 mile loop with a 70 foot climb, and swimming is not permitted.

items.title: Float the Winooski in a tube
items.teaser: $35 gets you a tube, a shuttle upriver and a 2.5 mile float back to Richmond
items.body: Umiak runs self guided tube floats on the Winooski River with the tube and shuttle included. The Richmond float covers 2.5 miles Thursday through Saturday, leaving at 10, 12 and 2, for $35 a person, and averages 2 to 3 hours depending on water levels. You meet at Overocker Park, 1301 Cochran Road, and the shuttle takes you upriver. In Waterbury, a 2 mile float runs Sunday through Wednesday. Add the $9 Tube and Brew voucher for a tasting flight at Stone Corral, or $5 for a creemee. Riders must be at least 6.

items.title: Paddle out onto Lake Champlain
items.teaser: Rent a kayak or board for $16 an hour, or catch a free dragon boat session
items.body: The Community Sailing Center, a waterfront nonprofit since 1994, rents kayaks, canoes and paddleboards for $16 an hour, first come first served with a two hour max, daily in high summer and on spring and fall weekends, for paddling the breakwater or out to North Beach or Lone Rock Point. The Burlington Surf Club at 50 Lakeside Ave, on the Hula campus, rents paddleboards for $25 an hour plus foil boards and windsurfers. Mālia, the dragon boat team based at the sailing center since 2013, paddles mid May to mid September and runs several free try it sessions each summer.

items.title: Sweat it out in a lakeside sauna or a spa
items.teaser: Book a private sauna by the lake, or join the $20 community sweat and dip in after
items.body: Savu Lakeside, on the Hula campus at 50 Lakeside Ave, rents two outdoor saunas privately by the hour, with changing rooms, robes and towels and an outdoor relaxation area, open from noon Monday through Thursday and from 9 Friday through Sunday. Its Hula Happy Hour community sessions run Tuesdays and Wednesdays from 5:30 to 6:30 for $20 a person, six people per sauna, with a dip in the lake between rounds. The Essex Resort & Spa at 70 Essex Way in Essex books massages and facials and has an indoor lap pool and an outdoor pool.

items.title: Take small kids swimming at Sand Bar
items.teaser: The sandy bottom stays shallow well out from a 2,000 foot beach in Milton
items.body: Sand Bar State Park in Milton, off U.S. Route 2, sits on a natural sandbar the Lamoille River built over tens of thousands of years, so the smooth, sandy bottom of Lake Champlain stays shallow well out from shore. Without it the lake here would be more than 150 feet deep. Vermont's most visited day use park has a 2,000 foot beach, a play area, grills, and kayak and paddleboard rentals, open Memorial Day weekend through Labor Day weekend, 10 to sunset. Day use is $5 for anyone 14 and up, $2 for kids 4 to 13. No pets.

items.title: Find a quiet trail close to town
items.teaser: A 3.5 mile pond loop, a lakeside ridge park, and a woods a few minutes from UVM
items.body: Centennial Woods is UVM's 70 acre natural area of conifers, streams and wetlands a few minutes' walk from campus, open to the public, with free weekend parking on Centennial Woods Way. Colchester Pond's 3.5 mile trail circles a mile long pond where beavers visit and signs of bobcat and moose turn up. Niquette Bay State Park climbs two ridges over 400 feet with views of Malletts Bay before dropping to Lake Champlain. Green Mountain Audubon Center in Huntington has five miles of trail through hemlock swamp and along the Huntington River, boardwalks at Peeper Pond and binoculars to borrow.

items.title: Ride Vermont's mountain bike trails
items.teaser: Flowy Saxon Hill near home, quarry trails for a $10 pass, and 100+ miles in East Burke
items.body: Close to town, the Fellowship of the Wheel maintains Sunny Hollow in Colchester, where the Blueberry and East loops suit beginners and ravines challenge stronger riders, and Saxon Hill in Essex, classic smooth and flowy singletrack on town land with the Flo, FreeFall and Extendo trails. Millstone Trails winds through 1,500 acres of historic quarries and regenerating forest around the Barre Town Forest, $10 a day for riders and free for walkers. Kingdom Trails in East Burke is a 100+ mile network that crosses more than 100 private landowners' properties, with day and annual memberships.

items.title: Spend a summer day out on the Champlain Islands
items.teaser: Swim at Knight Point, then picnic where the French built a fort in 1666
items.body: Take I-89 Exit 17 and follow Route 2 through South Hero, Grand Isle and North Hero, then Route 129 onto Isle La Motte. Knight Point State Park in North Hero has a summer swimming beach, a loop trail around the point and the rebuilt Knight Tavern, first built in 1790. On Isle La Motte, Saint Anne's Shrine sits on the lake where the French put up a fort and chapel in 1666, and the free Goodsell Ridge Fossil Preserve has a self guided tour of fossils from the Chazy Fossil Reef, open dawn to dusk, year round.

items.title: Spend a day in Montpelier, the smallest capital
items.teaser: Free State House tours, a $9 history museum next door, lunch at the co-op
items.body: The state calls Montpelier the smallest capital city in America, and the Vermont State House on State Street is the reason to go. Its House and Senate chambers are the oldest active legislative halls in the country that keep their original interiors. Borrow a free audio tour wand any time of year, join a free guided tour from July through October, or watch the session from January to May. Next door, the Vermont History Museum in the Pavilion Building is open Tuesday through Saturday, 10 to 4, $9 for adults. Hunger Mountain Co-op has a deli and cafe.

items.title: Spend a day in Middlebury and meet the Morgans
items.teaser: Morgan horses in Weybridge, a free college art museum and a bakery from 1986
items.body: The UVM Morgan Horse Farm in Weybridge, about an hour south of Burlington, has kept Morgans since Colonel Joseph Battell founded it in 1878, and more than 40 still live there. It opens daily 10 to 4 from May through October, $10 for adults in 2026, with guided or self guided tours. In town, the Middlebury College Museum of Art is free and open Tuesday through Sunday, and Otter Creek Bakery on College Street, a European style bakery and deli, has been baking since 1986.

items.title: Ski the independent hills
items.teaser: Night laps at Bolton, Cochran's nonprofit hill in Richmond, Mad River's Single Chair
items.body: Three hills near Burlington are still run by a family, a nonprofit or a co-op. Bolton Valley, founded in 1966 by Ralph DesLauriers and family owned, is Vermont's only resort with night skiing, typically Tuesday to Saturday until 10. Cochran's Ski Area in Richmond began in 1961 as Mickey and Ginny Cochran's backyard rope tow, became the nation's first nonprofit ski area, and is the home hill of Barbara Ann Cochran, 1972 Olympic gold, and Ryan Cochran-Siegle, Olympic silver in 2022 and 2026. Mad River Glen in Fayston is skier owned, bans snowboards and runs its 1948 Single Chair.

items.title: Cross-country ski out to a cabin in the woods
items.teaser: Ski to soup by the fire at von Trapp, or a cabin porch facing Camel's Hump
items.body: The von Trapp Outdoor Center in Stowe is the country's first cross-country ski center, with over 60 kilometers on 2,500 acres and the Slayton Pasture Cabin, where homemade soup, sandwiches and hot chocolate wait by a roaring fireplace. A 2026-27 adult pass is $33 on weekdays and $37 on weekends. Sleepy Hollow in Huntington grooms 32 kilometers, opens for night skiing on weeknights, and its Butternut Cabin, about a mile out, looks at Camel's Hump. Catamount in Williston, started by the McCullough family in 1978, grooms over 35 kilometers, and snowshoeing there is free.

items.title: Go public skating at a local rink
items.teaser: Public skate at Leddy Park for $5, with skate rentals for another $5
items.body: Burlington's city rink, the Gordon H. Paquette Ice Arena at Leddy Park, runs public skate sessions on weekday mornings and Sunday afternoons, posted on the city's recreation calendar. It costs $5 for adults, $4 for children and students and nothing for anyone 65 and up, and skate rentals are an extra $5 a pair. In South Burlington, the C. Douglas Cairns Recreation Arena on Swift Street posts its own public skating schedule.

items.title: Try ice fishing on Vermont's free day
items.teaser: No license needed on the last Saturday in January, and the state lends the gear
items.body: Vermont's Free Ice Fishing Day falls on the last Saturday in January every year, and anyone can fish any water open to ice fishing that day without a license. Vermont Fish and Wildlife pairs it with a free Ice Fishing Festival that moves around the state each winter, where staff and Let's Go Fishing instructors teach knots, baiting, tip-ups and ice safety, lend gear and run a fish fry. Their rule is at least three to four inches of clear black ice before you walk on it, and ice cleats are strongly recommended.

items.title: Skate across a frozen pond into the sea cave
items.teaser: Park at the high school, walk five minutes down, then glide 600 feet to the cave
items.body: The Donahue Sea Caves sit on a 15 acre Winooski Valley Park District tract off North Avenue, across from Burlington High School, mostly covered by a pond ringed with marsh. In summer you need a canoe or kayak to reach them, and in winter the frozen pond has become a popular skate. Per Seven Days, it's about a five minute walk down to the pond and roughly 600 feet along its edge to the cave, one big chamber of orange dolostone. Vermont Fish and Wildlife puts the minimum at three to four inches of clear black ice.

items.title: Jump in the lake for the Penguin Plunge
items.teaser: Raise $250 for Special Olympics Vermont, then run into Lake Champlain in February
items.body: Every winter, Special Olympics Vermont's Penguin Plunge sends a crowd into Lake Champlain at the Burlington Waterfront, and it's the organization's largest fundraiser. The 2026 plunge, the 31st, drew over 1,100 people and raised over $585,000. The 2027 plunge is Saturday, February 6, starting at 11. Every plunger commits to raising at least $250, or $150 for the Cool Schools Plunge, and the money lets athletes take part in sports and competitions at no cost. Plungers under 18 need a parent or guardian to sign the waiver.

items.title: Walk out to where the Winooski meets the lake
items.teaser: A half mile raised path through floodplain forest to rare sandy lakeshore
items.body: Delta Park is a 55 acre Winooski Valley Park District preserve in Colchester at the mouth of the Winooski River, with floodplain forest, marsh and over half a mile of natural sandy beach, uncommon on Lake Champlain and good turtle nesting habitat. A half mile elevated bike and footpath crosses it with views of the wetlands, the lake and the Adirondacks, and a bike bridge over the river mouth links it to Mayes Landing in Burlington on the Island Line. Audubon Vermont lists it among 17 Important Bird Areas in the state. Parking is a small lot off Windemere Way.

items.title: Drive Smugglers' Notch before winter closes it
items.teaser: Cliffs nearly 1,000 feet tall on a road too tight for long trucks, shut all winter
items.body: Route 108 north of Stowe squeezes through Smugglers' Notch, a narrow pass with cliffs rising nearly 1,000 feet on each side of a winding road the state closes in winter. Long trucks are banned by law, and some still get lodged between boulders every year. After the 1807 Embargo Act, locals herded cattle and carried goods through to Canada, and in the 1920s smugglers ran liquor. Barnes Camp Visitor Center starts the 3.5 mile scenic stretch, with a wetlands boardwalk, the Long Trail, the Smugglers' Notch Picnic Area by a stream and the Sterling Pond Trail.

items.title: Ride the dinner train down the Champlain Valley
items.teaser: Three courses cooked aboard on a three hour round trip from Burlington's station
items.body: Vermont Rail System's Champlain Valley Dinner Train boards at the Burlington Amtrak station platform at 1 Main Street for a three hour round trip to Middlebury and back, with a three course dinner made in the kitchen car and gratuity included. It runs Saturday and Sunday evenings in summer and adds Fridays in the fall, into late October. Tables seat up to four, guests must be 5 or older, entrees are chosen on board, and drinks from the full bar cost extra. The cars are climate controlled, with restrooms aboard.

items.title: Take a ghost walk through Burlington's dark side
items.teaser: Burlington's original ghost tour, written by the historian who started it in 2002
items.body: Queen City Ghostwalk is Burlington's original ghost tour, created in 2002 by Thea Lewis, the historian and author who writes every story you hear and came back to lead it in 2026. Tours run in the fall. Darkness Falls meets at the Democracy Sculpture on Courthouse Plaza, 199 Main Street, for theater ghosts, smugglers and serial killers, best for ten and up. Fright by Flashlight brings vintage ghost hunting tools into Lakeview Cemetery, and Ghosts and Legends of Lake Champlain starts at Union Station. Many walks sell out, so arrive 15 minutes early.

items.title: Hunt down the small, specific museums
items.teaser: Free snowflake photos in Jericho, a free maritime museum, an Underground Railroad farm
items.body: Jericho's Old Red Mill houses the free Snowflake Bentley Exhibit, with the original photographs and camera of Wilson Bentley, who on January 15, 1885 became the first person to photograph a single snow crystal. The Lake Champlain Maritime Museum in Vergennes is always free and open daily 10 to 4, May to October. Rokeby Museum in Ferrisburgh tells a nationally significant Underground Railroad story through four generations of the Robinson family, with trails open year round. The Hyde Log Cabin in Grand Isle, built in 1783, opens late May to Columbus Day.

items.title: See professional theater at Vermont Stage
items.teaser: More than 200 productions since 1994, opening each season with Winter Tales
items.body: Vermont Stage bills itself as northern Vermont's professional theatre company, and it has staged more than 200 productions since 1994. Shows play at 60 Lake Street, third floor, in Burlington. The 2026-27 season, its 32nd, opens with Winter Tales, December 9 to 13, when Patti Casey and friends bring back their annual run of funny and heartfelt stories and songs, and runs through May 23, 2027. The box office answers the phone Tuesday through Friday, noon to 5.

items.title: Collect the area's quirkiest landmarks
items.teaser: A 38 drawer filing cabinet, granite whale tails by I-89 and a sixteen sided church
items.body: Bren Alvarez put up File Under So. Co., Waiting for..., better known as the World's Tallest Filing Cabinet, for the 2002 South End Art Hop, 11 cabinets and 38 drawers, one for each year the Southern Connector had gone unbuilt since 1965. It now stands on a 10 foot pedestal at 208 Flynn Avenue. Jim Sardonis's black granite whale tails, Reverence, have dived into the grass beside I-89 in South Burlington since 1999. Richmond's Round Church, built in 1812 and 1813, is a sixteen sided meeting house and a National Historic Landmark.

items.title: Fix, borrow, or make something instead of buying it
items.teaser: A free monthly craft night, zipper swaps on Pine, $15 flat fixes, a library of things
items.body: Burlington is good at second lives. The Makery at 388 Pine Street sells secondhand art and craft supplies and hosts a free monthly Bring Your Own Craft Night with no registration. Further down Pine at 688, Sandbox repairs clothing, backpacks and technical outerwear and swaps busted zippers. Old Spokes Home on North Winooski Avenue makes used bikes and parts a specialty, with flat fixes from $15. And South Burlington's library lends games, tools and even a telescope from its Library of Things to cardholders 16 and up, nonresidents included.

items.title: Learn to contra dance on a Friday night
items.teaser: $12 to dance, a live band and a caller, and every single dance is taught
items.body: Queen City Contras has kept this old New England tradition going around Burlington for over thirty years. Dances run on select Fridays from 7 to 10 with a live band and a caller, every dance is taught, and no partner or experience is needed, so come at 6:45 for the beginner lesson. Bring clean soft soled shoes and water. It's $12, $5 for ages 12 to 18 or a limited budget, free under 12, and the hall moves between Burlington and Shelburne, so check the schedule.

items.title: Ride a ferry across the lake to New York
items.teaser: Walk on for $5.50 each way, Charlotte to Essex, with mountains on both shores
items.body: Lake Champlain Ferries has been crossing this lake since 1826, and walking on is the best cheap boat ride around, $5.50 each way for an adult and $12.25 with your car, before any fuel surcharge. From the Charlotte dock at 2901 Ferry Road it's about 25 minutes and 3 miles to Essex, New York, with the Adirondacks and the Green Mountains on either side. Up north, the Grand Isle to Plattsburgh crossing runs 24 hours a day, year round, in about 14 minutes. No reservations, so just show up 15 minutes early.

items.title: Swing an ice axe up a frozen waterfall
items.teaser: One day with AMGA certified guides on frozen waterfalls, technical gear included
items.body: Petra Cliffs, the Burlington climbing gym, takes beginners outside from December through March for a one day Intro to Ice Climbing in groups of one to six. Guides certified by the AMGA teach crampon and ice axe technique on frozen waterfalls and bring the harness, helmet, ropes and other technical gear. You bring warm layers, food, water and your own ride, and your guide sends the exact meeting spot before the day.

items.title: Eat your way through the Champlain Valley Fair
items.teaser: Ten days of midway rides, a livestock barn and free grandstand shows, back August 27, 2027
items.body: The Champlain Valley Fair calls itself Vermont's largest annual event, ten days at the Champlain Valley Expo at 105 Pearl Street in Essex Junction. The 2027 fair runs August 27 to September 5, noon to 10 on weekdays and 10 to 10 on weekends, with midway rides, a concert series, motor sports and free grandstand shows with paid admission. The 2026 free lineup included sheep shearing in the Livestock Barn, a daily parade, a BMX stunt show and Old McDonald's Farm, where kids could milk a cow. Parking is $10 cash, and tickets sell only through Etix.

items.title: Run or cheer the Vermont City Marathon
items.teaser: May 30, 2027, with relays for teams of 2 or 3 to 5 and a downhill finish at the lake
items.body: The Vermont City Marathon, founded in 1989 and the first US marathon to add a relay, is Vermont's largest single day sporting event, with more than 5,000 participants and 20,000 spectators on Memorial Day weekend. The 38th running is May 30, 2027, on a new two loop course along the Church Street Marketplace and the bike path, with Taiko drummers and a downhill finish past Union Station into Waterfront Park. Run the full, the new half, or a 2 person ($185) or 3 to 5 person ($240) relay at early bird prices through December 31, 2026.

items.title: Throw a round of disc golf
items.teaser: A 9 basket woods course in South Burlington, then courses ranked #6 and #8 by UDisc
items.body: Disc golf around Burlington runs from a neighborhood woods course to two of the best in the world. Awasiwi Woods, behind Munsen Field at the South Burlington middle and high school campus, is South Burlington's first disc golf course, 9 baskets with grey tees for short rounds and blue tees for long ones, open dawn to dusk. The South Burlington Public Library lends disc sets for up to 2 weeks. Smugglers' Notch Resort has Brewster Ridge and Fox Run Meadows, ranked #6 and #8 by UDisc, plus the Village 9, playable in 30 minutes to an hour.

items.title: Make a bakery run beyond downtown
items.teaser: Creme brulee cake in South Burlington, 60 kinds of pie in Underhill, Red Hen bread
items.body: Three bakeries are worth the drive. Mirabelles at 3060 Williston Road in South Burlington is known for its best seller, a creme brulee cake of chiffon and vanilla custard. Poorhouse Pies bakes over 60 varieties of full size pies daily at its Underhill pie shop on Route 15, plus pocket pies that run out fast. Red Hen Baking, founded in Duxbury in 1999, now bakes in Middlesex, where its self serve Bread Box stand sells its most popular breads and pastries from 8 to 5. Its loaves include the Miche and Kingdom Rye, and the cafe is in Montpelier.

items.title: Stop at a real Vermont general store
items.teaser: A Jericho store open since 1807, Charlotte's Old Brick and Shelburne's penny candy
items.body: The Jericho Center Country Store at 25 Jericho Center Circle calls itself Vermont's longest running store, in business since 1807, with breakfast, a deli and a grill, open 7 to 7 on weekdays. The Old Brick Store at 290 Ferry Road in Charlotte is a 170-year-old general store reborn as a café and shop with a coffee program, natural wines and made-to-order breakfast and lunch, closed every Tuesday. The Shelburne Country Store at 29 Falls Road, a general store since 1886 in a building from about 1835, makes its own fudge and sells penny candy, daily 10 to 5.

items.title: Walk or bike the Stowe Recreation Path
items.teaser: 5.3 paved miles along the West Branch, partly paid for by selling it at $2 an inch
items.body: The Stowe Recreation Path is a 5.3 mile paved greenway from Stowe Village to Topnotch Resort on the Mountain Road, crossing back and forth over the West Branch of Little River. The first 2.7 miles were built by 1984 on 27 donated easements, and the full path was done in 1989, partly paid for by selling pieces at $2 per inch. Since 2011 the town has kept it open all year for walkers, runners, bikers, snowshoers, cross country skiers and rollerbladers. Lintilhac Park, behind the Stowe Community Church, is one of four parking spots.

title: The Perfect Burlington Saturday
tagline: One ideal day in the city, hour by hour.
intro:
This is the sequence that shows Burlington at its best — market, water, South End, dinner, a show. It's built for a warm-season Saturday; in winter, skip the causeway ride and the waterfront lunch, and lean on the South End taprooms, the Fleming, and a fireside dinner instead.

Everything here links to the full details. Adjust freely — the point is the shape of the day, not the exact clock.

items.title: Breakfast worth the small wait
items.body: Start slow. Handy's has fed Burlington from the same Maple Street counter for generations, and the Friendly Toast does all-day retro brunch a block off Church Street. A short line at either is a good sign, not a deterrent.

items.title: Graze the farmers market
items.body: Saturday mornings the market fills with Vermont produce, wood-fired everything, and cider slushies. Eat your way down one side and don't plan lunch too early — half the city is moving at quarter speed and you should too.

items.title: Take the waterfront while the light's good
items.body: Walk down to the yellow porch swings facing the Adirondacks. This is the postcard, and it's free every day of the year. Sit for longer than you planned.

items.title: Bike straight out onto the lake
items.body: Rent from Local Motion at the boathouse and ride the Greenway onto the Island Line causeway — a rail bed three miles into open water, lake on both sides. Turn around whenever; in summer the bike ferry carries you across the cut to the islands.

items.title: Lunch with your feet near the water
items.body: Back at the harbor, eat where the lake is the view — Skinny Pancake's crepes and sunset-odds patio, or Splash's floating deck if you want a drink with it.

items.title: Pine Street: beer, art, and molten glass
items.body: Trade the water for the South End. Zero Gravity's patio and Switchback's unchanged flagship are two blocks apart, the Soda Plant's studios and roastery are a short walk, and AO Glass has artisans working if you time it right. Pace yourself; dinner's coming.

items.title: Dinner you'll bring up for months
items.body: Book ahead. Honey Road's mezze and Hen of the Wood's mushroom toast are the two tables people plan trips around; Leunig's bistro corner is the see-and-be-seen classic if you want Church Street energy.

items.title: A show, then find the unmarked door
items.body: Catch stand-up at the Vermont Comedy Club or whatever's loud at Red Square, which runs live music nearly every night. Close it out at Lincoln's, the five-dollar-everything speakeasy whose entrance you have to find yourself. Now you know it's there.

title: A Perfect Day on the Water
tagline: Sunrise bagel to sunset sail — the summer lake day.
intro: Burlington's whole reason for being is the lake, and on the right summer day you can build an entire itinerary that never leaves its edge. This one runs paddle to beach to causeway to sunset sail. Sunscreen is the only hard requirement.

items.title: Coffee and a bagel to carry
items.body: Fuel first. Myer's wood-fired Montreal-style bagels are the local pick, and Scout pairs serious coffee with house-made ice cream for later ideas. Get it to go — the water's waiting.

items.title: Paddle out before the wind picks up
items.body: The Community Sailing Center rents kayaks and paddleboards right on the harbor — mornings are glassy and calm, the best window to get out on Champlain under your own power. No boat of your own required.

items.title: Ride the causeway to the islands
items.body: Grab a bike from Local Motion and ride the Island Line straight into the lake. In season the bike ferry drops you in South Hero — pedal on to Snow Farm Vineyard for a mid-ride glass and, some afternoons, live music on the lawn.

items.title: Claim a patch of beach
items.body: Burlington keeps real sand inside the city. North Beach has the scene and a tiki bar, Oakledge has the swimming cove and the accessible treehouse, Leddy has the elbow room. Pick by mood; the water's the same.

items.title: A creemee by the lake, non-negotiable
items.body: Vermont's maple soft-serve, eaten within sight of the water, is the whole point of summer here. The waterfront windows handle the classic; walk it off along the boardwalk.

items.title: Sunset — under sail or over a Foam beer
items.body: Two great ways to take the golden hour: a BYOB sunset sail on the Whistling Man schooner, or a world-class IPA on Foam's lakeside patio as the sky lights up behind the Adirondacks.

items.title: Dinner on the dock
items.body: End where you spent the day. Splash floats on the harbor, the Spot on the Dock does surf-shack tables at the water's edge, and Shanty's fried perch is the old-school move. Sunset seats go first.

title: Burlington in the Snow
tagline: How locals actually love a Vermont winter day.
intro:
Winter is not the off-season here — it's just a different set of moves. This day trades the beach for groomed trails, a warm bowl, a museum, and the hot-cold ritual that makes February bearable. Dress in layers and lean in.

One honest caution: the sea-caves stop only exists after a long, hard freeze. Never walk out on early-season ice, and never go alone.

items.title: A slow coffee in the warmest room in town
items.body: Ease in at Muddy Waters — all wood, plants, and low light, the cabin-like café built for exactly this kind of gray morning. Read something. There's no rush.

items.title: Get outside anyway
items.body: The trick to Vermont winter is going out into it. Catamount grooms fat-bike and snowshoe loops fifteen minutes away, Bolton Valley is the locals' ski hill (with night skiing later), and the Intervale's flat farm trails take cross-country skis right inside the city.

items.title: Warm up around a bowl of ramen
items.body: Come in from the cold to Gaku's rich tonkotsu — the single most restorative lunch in the city when it's ten degrees out. The January line out the door makes the case better than we can.

items.title: An afternoon that isn't cold
items.body: Bank some indoor hours. The Fleming's collection is nearly yours alone on a weekday, and ECHO's lake tanks are a reliable win with kids when the waterfront's a frozen wind tunnel.

items.title: Walk out to the sea caves — if the lake allows
items.body: In a deep-freeze winter, locals walk across solid ice to the Donahue Sea Caves near the river delta — a destination that only exists a few weeks a year. Only attempt this after sustained hard cold, with company, never early season. When conditions are right, there's nothing else like it.

items.title: Sauna, then the plunge
items.body: The Nordic answer to a cold day: book a private wood-fired sauna at Savu by the lake, cycle hot to cold, and — if you've earned your nerve — drop through a hole in the frozen lake itself.

items.title: Fireside pint, then the Gut
items.body: Thaw out by the Farmhouse's basement fireplace with a Vermont beer, then head up to Gutterson for UVM hockey — one of college hockey's loudest old barns, and the best cheap winter night in town.

title: Free Burlington
tagline: Everything worth doing that costs nothing.
intro: Burlington punches above its size on free things to do — parks, public art, beach access, live music, and galleries that don't charge admission. This list updates automatically from the master list whenever we verify a free entry.

title: Cheap Eats & Drinks
tagline: A $15 budget gets you farther than you think in Vermont.
intro:
Burlington's food scene skews toward quality over price, but there are enough places where you can eat and drink well without watching the tab. Single-dollar sign means a good meal under $20; most are under $15.

The best value in the city is almost always a pint and something at one of the South End taprooms — Zero Gravity's Clean State pilsner and Citizen Cider's Wit's Up are both under $8 and better than anything you'd pay three times as much for somewhere else.

title: Rainy Day Burlington
tagline: Vermont weather is variable. Here's the plan B.
intro: Burlington averages 155 cloudy days per year. The upside: more excuses to visit the Fleming, nurse a beer at a South End taproom, or finally make it to ECHO. This list covers everything indoor-friendly that's worth your time when the Adirondacks disappear into the clouds.

title: Date Night in Burlington
tagline: From a first dinner to the kind of evening you remember.
intro:
Burlington is easy to be romantic in — the lake does a lot of the work. These picks range from a Skinny Pancake patio lunch with good sunset odds, to Leunig's bistro for something properly sit-down, to a Vermont Comedy Club show that breaks the ice without needing you to.
